          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
ASSAM
1. We have heard Mr. Rishi Malhotra, learned amicus curiae and Ms. Nimisha
Menon, learned counsel appearing for the State of Assam.
2. Our attention has been drawn to the affidavit dated 06 th April, 2026, filed
by the Officer on Special Duty in the  office  of the  Resident Commissioner,
Assam Bhawan.
3. We express our displeasure at the affidavit having been sworn by the
Officer on Special Duty in the office of the Resident Commissioner. He cannot
have any direct knowledge of what is happening in the State of Assam pursuant
to orders passed by this Court.
4. We would expect that the affidavit, which we propose to direct the State
of Assam to file in terms of the direction hereunder, is affirmed by a responsible
officer in the Education Department, Government of Assam.
5. Reference  has  been  made  to  contractual  teachers  working  under  the
jurisdiction of Samagra Siksha, Assam at the block level.
6. It is not indicated as to whether the resource persons, or the assistant
resource persons, are qualified or not in terms of Rehabilitation Council of India1
stipulations.
7. It is also not indicated as to whether the Screening Committee, which has
been constituted vide notification dated 28 th July 2025 pursuant to this Court’s
1  RCI
13

--- Page 52 ---
order dated 7th March 2025, has considered the case of any contractual teacher
duly qualified to teach children with special needs.
8. We strongly disapprove the indifference and apathy shown by the State of
Assam to assist this Court by not placing proper facts and figures, as well as by
not complying with this Court’s orders.
9. Our attention has also been drawn to a previous affidavit dated 16 th April,
2024,  where  the  State  of  Assam  had  referred  to  255  Special  Educators
possessing RCI qualification having been appointed on contractual basis. Fate of
these 255 Special Educators is unknown.
10. We  direct  the  State  of  Assam  to  have  the  credentials  of  these  255
candidates verified by asking them to appear before the Screening Committee
within three weeks from date.
11. The Screening Committee shall proceed to give a decision within two
weeks thereafter.
12. The State of Assam is granted six weeks’ time to file a better affidavit.
13. Within this period of six weeks, the Screening Committee must ensure
that the task entrusted to it by this order is accomplished.
14. We hope and trust that within this period, maximum number of teachers
having the requisite qualifications shall be appointed bearing in mind the earlier
order dated 7th March, 2025 also.
15. The outcome shall be indicated in the affidavit which is to be filed in terms
of the earlier direction.
RAJASTHAN:
16. We are informed that the number of sanctioned posts in the State of
14

--- Page 53 ---
Rajasthan is 4399. In paragraph 4 of the affidavit dated 29 th November, 2025, it
is stated that 4109 RCI qualified regularly selected and appointed teaches are
presently working in the State leaving a balance of 290 posts which are unfilled.
We are further informed that an advertisement has been issued on 22 nd May,
2026 calling for applications from eligible interested aspirants and the process
is underway.
17. In such view of the matter, we grant liberty to the State of Rajasthan to fill
up the balance 290 posts strictly in accordance with merit.  An action taken
report shall be filed in the form of an affidavit within four weeks.
CHHATTISGARH:
18. Issue notice on Interlocutory Application No. 213132/2026 (application for
intervention).
19. Notice is accepted by Ms. Ankita Sharma, learned counsel.  Service of
formal notice on the respondent – State of Chhattisgarh is dispensed with.
20. Mr. K.M. Nataraj,  learned Additional  Solicitor  General representing  the
State of Chhattisgarh shall obtain appropriate instructions as to whether the
State, by amending the rules for recruitment, has included Teachers Eligibility
Test2 as an essential qualification for appointment of Special Educators.
21. An up-to-date status of appointment process shall also be indicated by
filing a status report in the form of an affidavit, to be filed by 3rd August, 2026.
BIHAR:
22. Mr.  Manish  Kumar,  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State  of  Bihar
submits that TET is a mandatory requirement of the Bihar State School Teacher
2  TET
15

--- Page 54 ---
(Appointment, Transfer, Disciplinary Proceedings and Service Conditions) Rules,
20233 and applies squarely to Special School Teachers as defined in Rule 2(xvii)
thereof.
23. Having perused Rule 5 of the 2023 Rules, we find that the qualification of
a Special School Teacher shall be such as prescribed by the RCI.
24. The marginal note “Essential qualification for appointment to the post of
School Teacher” has to be read and understood bearing in mind the definition of
School Teacher in Rule 2(xvii) of the 2023 Rules, which does not include a
Special School Teacher. Special School Teacher, as noticed above, is separately
defined in Rule 2(xviii) of the 2023 Rules.
25. We are prima facie of the view that insistence of the State of Bihar that
contractual  teachers  should  possess  TET  qualification,  in  addition  to  RCI
qualification, is beyond the requirement of the 2023 Rules.
26. We  would  have  proceeded  to  pass  an  appropriate  order  today  but
accepting the request of Mr. Manish Kumar, we adjourn hearing for a week.
27. Unless we are persuaded to hold that the stipulations of Rule 5 of the
2023 Rules are applicable to Special School Teachers, we shall proceed to direct
the State to issue appointment letters to all the 649 plus 05 candidates who
have RCI qualification.
28. If the State of Bihar is so advised, a further status report may be filed by
3rd August, 2026.
29. Issue notice on IA No. 198134/2026, being an application for direction.
Notice is accepted by Mr. Manish Kumar.  Service of formal notice on the State
is dispensed with.

posts  of  Special  Education  Teachers  whereas  for  the  upper  primary  and
secondary sections, the number is 727; out of these, 251 and 261 are the
number of posts vacant in respect of the aforesaid two sections, respectively.
34. A statement has been made in the affidavit that persons who have been
engaged as Inclusive Education Resource Persons (IERP) on contract basis and
having necessary qualifications for appointment as Special Teachers have been
allowed to participate in the recruitment process. This, prima facie, appears to
be contrary to the letter and spirit of the order dated 7 th March,2025 passed by
this Court.
35. It is also apparent from such affidavit that no Screening Committee has
been constituted for the purpose of screening the contractual teachers which,
also, is in violation of the order dated 7th March, 2025.
36. The State of Telangana would be well advised to follow the order dated 7 th
March, 2025, constitute a Screening Committee and screen all such teachers
who have been employed as IERP by the next date of hearing.
37. Once the process of consideration by the Screening Committee of these
IERPs  is  complete  and appointments  are  made  on  the  vacant posts, noted
above, shall the remaining vacant posts be filled up by the State.

5. Challenge in this batch of appeals is to the
orders passed by the learned Single Judge and the Full

the sake of convenience, we treat the appeals arising
out of the SLP(C) Nos. 10872-10898/2024 as the lead
case which arises out of the Full Bench judgment of the
Patna High Court. The Full Bench was constituted as the
matter was refereed to a larger Bench noticing the
controversy  as  to  the  acquisition  of  Diploma  in
Elementary Education; the minimum qualification for
appointment  of  teachers  in  the  primary  school  as
prescribed by the NCTE. Since, there were divergence in

--- Page 77 ---
3
opinion  by  different  Benches  of  the  High  Court,
including the Single Judge and the Division Bench, the
Full Bench took up the matter so as to give a quietus
to the issue at the High Court level.
6. In the present batch of appeals, there are
appellants who were appointed prior to 31.03.2015 and
thereafter also. The Full Bench, in the operative part
of the impugned judgment, passed the following order/
directions:
“41. On the interpretation given by us to Section
23(1), we issue the following directions:-
 
(1) those who were appointed prior to 01.04.2010 who
have  acquired  the  teaching  qualification  on  or
before 08.08.2021 would be entitled to be continued;
(2) the results withheld, when declared, if it
relates back to the period before 08.08.2021, those
persons should be continued in employment;
 
(3) the issuance of certificates also would have to
concede to the date of publication of results; which
if published before 08.08.2021, those persons will
be deemed to have been continued;
(4) the unqualified teachers who were appointed
during  the  relaxation  period,  i.e.  between
01.04.2010 and 31.03.2015 will also be deemed to
have been continued, if they have acquired the
teachers  training  qualification;  the  minimum
qualification, on or before 08.08.2021.
(5)  The  persons,  who  were  appointed  after
31.03.2015, if are unqualified will have to be
terminated  even  if,  they  have  acquired  the
qualification  within  08.08.2021;  since  their
appointment itself is invalid. There could not have
been  any  unqualified  persons  appointed  after
31.03.2015.
(6)  Those  who  were  in  place  as  teachers  on
01.04.2010 and then on 31.03.2015, if not acquired
the  qualification  before  08.08.2021  will  stand
terminated.”

--- Page 78 ---
4
7. Insofar as the unqualified teachers appointed
after  31.03.2015  are  concerned,  since  their
appointment,  at  the  inception,  were  illegal  for
violating Section-23(1) of the  Right of Children to
Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (for short,
‘the RTE Act’), the Full Bench has rightly concluded
that their appointments cannot be saved by allowing
them to continue and acquire qualification within an
extended time frame.
8. Upon  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant(s), who are aggrieved by the dismissal of
their petitions/appeals by the High Court, we are in
agreement with the reasoning assigned and thus, such
appellants in the present batch of appeals, who were
appointed after  31.03.2015, have  no case  in their
favour and their appeals are dismissed.
9. In respect of such teachers, who were in service
on  or  before  31.03.2015,  the  High  Court,  by  the
impugned judgment, has extended the time for acquiring
the qualification of Diploma in Elementary Education
(D.El.Ed) within  08.08.2021 and  the said  batch of
teachers have been allowed to continue in service till
they  acquire  such  qualification  on  or  before
08.08.2021.
10. Mr. Vikas Singh and Mr. Santosh Kumar, learned
senior counsels and other learned counsel appearing for
the appellants, who were in service on 31.03.2015,
would submit that their case is covered by judgments

--- Page 79 ---
5
rendered by this Court in: (i) Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust Vs. State of Maharashtra and Ors. (2025 SCC
Online SC 1912) and (ii) State of U.P. Vs. Anjuman
Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust & Ors. (2026 SCC online SC 998).
11. In the first judgment,  Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem
Trust (supra), this Court, while dealing with the issue
of  acquiring  the  minimum  qualification  of  Teacher
Eligibility Test (TET), directed that insofar as in
service teachers recruited prior to the enactment of
the RTE Act, i.e. 31.03.2015, and having more than 05
years to retire on superannuation are concerned, they
shall be under an obligation to qualify TET within two
years from the date (01.09.2025) on which the judgment
was delivered, in order to continue in service. If any
of such teachers fail to qualify the TET within the
time granted by this Court, they shall have to quit
service. For the sake of clarity, paragraph- 217 of the
first Anjuman Ishaat-E-Taleem Trust judgment (supra) is
extracted below:
“217. Insofar as in-service teachers recruited
prior to enactment of the RTE Act and having
more than 5 years to retire on superannuation
are  concerned,  they  shall  be  under  an
obligation to qualify the TET within 2 years
from date in order to continue in service. If
any of such teachers fail to qualify the TET
within the time that we have allowed, they
shall  have  to  quit  service.  They  may  be
compulsorily  retired;  and  paid  whatever
terminal benefits they are entitled to. We add
a  rider  that  to  qualify  for  the  terminal
benefits, such teachers must have put in the

--- Page 80 ---
6
qualifying period of service, in accordance
with the rules. If any teacher has not put in
the  qualifying  service  and  there  is  some
deficiency, his/her case may be considered by
the appropriate department in the Government
upon a representation being made by him/her.”
12. Thereafter,  in  the  second  Anjuman  Ishaat-E-
Taleem Trust (supra), the time allowed for acquiring
the TET qualification was extended by 31.08.2028 by
observing thus:
“32.  Having  regard  to  the  paramountcy  of
ensuring continuity in elementary education of
children,  we  deem  it  appropriate  to  grant
limited relief by extending the period earlier
stipulated for acquiring the TET qualification,
again, in exercise of our power under Article
142 of the Constitution.
33. Appreciating that the TET examination must
be  conducted  by  the  relevant  authorities
expeditiously as well as the time and resources
required for the same are limited, we alter and
extend the timeline granted in paragraph 217
of Anjuman (supra) for in-service teachers to
acquire the TET qualification from 2 (two) to 3
(three) years, i.e., the qualification has to be
obtained  by  31 st August,  2028  instead  of
31st August, 2027, as originally directed.
34. Needless to observe, it shall also be the
endeavour  of  the  respective  States  and  the
competent  authorities  to  conduct  the  TET
periodically, and preferably twice every year,
interspersed with an approximate period of six
months between the successive examinations, so
as to afford eligible teachers a reasonable
opportunity  to  comply  with  the  statutory
requirement.
35. We make it abundantly clear that no further
prayer  for  extension  of  time  shall  be
entertained.”
13. Although,  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
State  of  Bihar  made  efforts  to  distinguish  the

--- Page 81 ---
7
judgments rendered by this Court in Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem Trust (supra), however, after sometime, learned
counsel  agreed  that  like  TET,  D.El.Ed  is  also  an
essential qualification.
14. In our considered view, since TET and D.El.Ed
both are essential qualification for appointment as
teachers at the primary school level, the direction
contained  in  Anjuman  Ishaat-E-Taleem  Trust  can  be
applied in the present cases also.
15. There is no dispute that D.El.Ed is an essential
qualification  and  thus,  once  the  appellants  were
lacking in that qualification but, were in service on
31.03.20215, the time extended in   Anjuman Ishaat-E-
Taleem Trust squarely applies for them also and thus,
we dispose of all such appeals in which the appellants
were in service on 31.03.2015, allowing them time to
acquire  the  D.El.ED  qualification  on  or  before
31.08.2028. Those candidates, who were appointed prior
to 31.03.2015 but, have been terminated in terms of the
High Court order, shall be allowed to continue so that
they are given time to acquire the qualification on or
before  31.08.2028. The result of D.El.Ed examination
held already shall be declared at the earliest.
16. We make it abundantly clear that no further
extension of time will be entertained.
17. The appeals are accordingly disposed of, in the
above terms.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
SLP (Criminal) No.2729 of 2026
1. List on 27.07.2026.
W.P. (Criminal) No.329 of 2023
2. By order dated 26.02.2026, this Court took note of the fact
7

--- Page 95 ---
that the victims and their families, who continue to reside in the
State of Manipur, were unaware of the filing of the chargesheets,
because the judicial proceedings were being conducted before the
competent Court at Guwahati. Consequently, directions were issued
by this Court for extending free legal aid to the victims and for
supplying copies of the chargesheets to them through their legal
aid  counsel.  Subsequently,  vide an  order  dated  24.03.2026,
compliance with the aforesaid directions was reiterated.
3. Thereafter, as noticed in our order dated 27.05.2026, a status
report was submitted by Hon’ble the Chief Justice of High Court of
Manipur. The report, inter-alia, stated that the Registrar Generals
of the High Courts of Manipur and Guwahati, together with the
Member Secretaries of the State Legal Services Authority of both
States, had established communication with the victims and their
families to facilitate the provision of free legal aid. It further
recorded that a structured course of action had been evolved in a
joint meeting regarding the appointment of legal aid counsel,
supply  of  chargesheets,  and  addressing  logistical  impediments
relating to travel, boarding and lodging, amongst other issues.
4. We are informed by Ms. Vrinda Grover, learned counsel for the
petitioner(s) that notwithstanding the aforesaid directions and the
status report filed by Hon’ble the Chief Justice of the High Court
of Manipur, several victims’ families have conveyed that copies of
the chargesheets have still not been supplied to them. She further
submits that she was able to contact two legal aid counsel, of whom
one had received the chargesheet, whereas the other was still
awaiting its supply.  
8

--- Page 96 ---
5. We accordingly direct that the legal aid counsel, with the aid
of the Member Secretaries of the State Legal Services Authority of
Manipur and Guwahati to immediately co-orindate with the offices of
Hon’ble the Chief Justices of High Court of Manipur and Guwahati
for obtaining the copies of the chargesheets, wherever the same
have been filed but have not yet been supplied to the victims,
their families, or their legal aid counsel. It goes without saying
that the concerned authorities shall ensure that such chargesheets
are supplied at the earliest, and in any event not later than one
week from the date on which the request is received from the legal
aid counsel.
6. Mr. Dattatray Padsalgikar, former Director General of Police,
Maharashtra, who was appointed by this Court to monitor the ongoing
investigations, has filed his 14 th status report dated 15.07.2026.
The report reveals that a new Director General of Police has been
appointed in the State of Manipur. It refers to the violent
incident that occurred on 13.05.2026 and its aftermath.  The report
further notes, as a positive development towards the restoration of
peace and communal harmony, the visit of the Hon’ble Chief Minister
of Manipur to Churachandpur on 04.07.2026 to attend the funeral of
a Member of Legislative Assembly, who had died due to the injuries
sustained by him in the 2023 violence. The report additionally
highlights joint operations are being undertaken by the State
Police and the Central Security Forces to maintain law and order,
and further records that security along the National Highways has
been strengthened to ensure uninterrupted movement of essential
commodities.
9

--- Page 97 ---
7. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), to whom 31 cases
were transferred by the State Government for investigation, has
also filed its status report. The report, inter-alia, notes that
chargesheets have been filed in 21 cases; investigation is ongoing
in 11 cases; closure reports have been filed in 6 cases, of which 3
have been accepted; and 4 cases are under investigation. The
complete particulars have been furnished in a tabulated form
annexed to the report.
8. The  CBI  has  also  highlighted  the  following  challenges
encountered during the course of investigation:
(i) Owing to the volatile law and order situation, examination of
witnesses  has  become  difficult,  as  many  of  them  have  been
displaced/relocated.
(ii) Several witnesses have been reluctant to cooperate due to an
atmosphere of mistrust.
(iii)  The existence of multiple regional dialects and language
barriers  has  posed  significant  difficulties  in  effectively
communicating with local residents and witnesses.
(iv)  The prolonged suspension of internet services has adversely
affected the collection of digital evidence.
(v)  Restrictions on the free movement of persons have also impeded
the conduct of field investigations.
9. Special Investigation Teams (SITs), who are investigating 3020
cases across 8 districts, have likewise filed their status report.
It records that chargesheets have been filed in 301 cases; charges
have been framed in 31 cases; and trial has commenced in 10 cases.
In all these cases, as many as 2924 witnesses are yet to be
10

--- Page 98 ---
examined.  The  complete  particulars  have  been  appended  in  a
tabulated form in the status report.
10. We are further informed that an online meeting was convened on
29.06.2026 with the Director General of Police, Manipur and other
senior police officials, wherein emphasis was laid on initiating
appropriate action against more than 800 identified accused persons
and ensuring the filing of chargesheets these cases. The senior
officials  were  accordingly  advised  to  expedite  the  ongoing
investigations.
11. It may be true that on account of the challenges highlighted
by the CBI, they might be facing some practical difficulties in
carrying the ongoing investigations to their logical conclusion.
Nevertheless, we are of the view that the pending investigations
must be completed within a reasonable timeframe. We are, therefore,
tentatively proposing the constitution of Special Courts, with the
concurrence of the State of Manipur and the High Courts of Manipur
and Guwahati, so that the trials can be conducted on a day-to-day
basis, especially in light of the fact that there has already been
an inordinate delay in completing the investigation of pending
cases. This course of action, however, would be possible only after
the CBI and the SITs conclude their respective investigations and
file the requisite chargesheets. We, therefore, impress upon both
investigating  agencies  to  make  all  possible  endeavours,
irrespective of the impediments referred to above, to complete the
investigations expeditiously.
12. In this regard, we direct the State of Manipur, through its
Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, to provide full
11

--- Page 99 ---
cooperation to the investigating agencies, coordinate effectively
with them, and provide all such assistance as may reasonably be
required to overcome the difficulties highlighted in the status
reports above.
13. Let  fresh  status  reports  be  filed  by  Mr.  Dattatray
Padsalgikar, the CBI and the SITs before the next date of hearing.
14. We have also requested Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, learned ASG
representing the State of Manipur and the CBI to collate the
details of all the FIRs in which investigations are pending or
where chargesheets have already been filed. This would give an
estimated  idea  of  how  many  trials  would  be  required  to  be
conducted. This information is imminently required as it would
enable this Court to assess the requisite strength and the number
of Special Courts which need to be established for conducting the
trials.
15. On oral mentioning, IA (D) No.15531/2026 (in W.P. (Civil)
No.540/2023) is taken on Board.
16. Learned counsel for the applicant(s) points out that at least
30 persons belonging to one community are missing and that, despite
efforts from the concerned organisation, their whereabouts could
not be ascertained.
17. In  this  regard,  we  deem  it  appropriate  to  direct  the
applicant(s) to approach Hon’ble the Chief Justice of the High
Court of Manipur, who may, in his discretion, entrust the task of
tracing the missing persons to one of the SITs or to such other
authority or forum as the Chief Justice may deem appropriate.

NON-REPORTABLE 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026 
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL.) NO.6358 OF 2026) 
 
 
SANGIT @ CHHOTU  … APPELLANT(S) 
  
VERSUS 
 
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA … RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH, J. 
 
1. Leave granted. 
 
2. The present appeal assails the judgment and 
order dated 10.10.2025 by the High Court of 
Judicature at Bombay, Nagpur Bench in 
Criminal Appeal No.563/2004 whereby the 
High Court affirmed the order of conviction of 
the appellant herein passed by the 1st Ad  hoc 
Additional Sessions Judge, Wardha on 

--- Page 102 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 2 of 12 
02.09.2004 under sections 304 -II and 324 of 
the Indian Penal Code,1860 (hereinafter, ‘IPC’). 
  
3. The proceedings arose from a complaint dated 
03.07.2002, filed by one Vinod Ganeshlal 
Chaudhary who alleged that at about 5:45 pm 
on the same day, when he and his maternal 
uncle Ramesh Prajapati were returning on 
motorcycle from the funeral of his relative , the 
appellant herein came from behind in his jeep 
and dashed against them with the intention to 
kill them due to existing political rivalry between 
them. It was stated that the appellant herein 
was driving the jeep while his brothers Sanjay 
and Vijay Ramteke were sitting by his side. Both 
the complainant, who was the pillion rider, and 
his uncle, fell on the road and sustained 
injuries. Thereafter, Ramesh Prajapati was 
taken to the hospital where he succumbed to 
the injuries. 
 
4. An FIR bearing Crime No.93/2002 came to be 
registered in this regard under sections 302 and 
307 read with section 34 of the IPC and the 

--- Page 103 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 3 of 12 
police, along with the panch witnesses, 
proceeded to the spot for investigation. During 
the spot investigation, it was noticed that tyre  
marks of skidding were visible on the road up to 
the distance of 44 meters. After the end of tyre 
marks, dried up stains of blood could be seen 
on the road. The blood samples were taken and 
collected in a small bottle and a seizure memo 
was prepared in th is regard. It was also 
observed that a Suzuki motorcycle was lying on 
the road in a damaged condition, with the back 
portion pressed, the rear wheel, rim, and 
indicators broken, and both rear shock 
absorbers damaged. 
 
5. Thereafter, the police proceeded to seize the jeep 
belonging to the appellant parked at the front of 
the house of the co -accused Sanjay Ramteke. 
Upon inspection of the jeep, it was found that 
the radiator and iron mudguard of the jeep on 
the front side wer e pressed, and both the 
indicators were broken. Pertinently, there were 
also broken pieces of red coloured glass of the 

--- Page 104 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 4 of 12 
indicator of the Suzuki motorcycle entangled 
near the radiator. 
 
6. The postmortem of the body of the deceased was 
also conducted and the Medical Officer on duty 
gave the opinion that the death was caused due 
to hypovolemic shock from multiple injuries. 
The Medical Officer also examined the injured 
complainant Vinod Chaudh ari and it was 
observed that he had multiple abrasions on the 
back. 
 
7. The seized articles and samples were sent for 
forensic analysis, statements were recorded, 
and after due investigation a chargesheet was 
filed before the Judicial Magistrate, Wardha. 
Since the offences under sections 302 and 307 
read with section 34 of the  IPC were found 
triable by the Court of Sessions, the matter 
came to be committed to the Court of Sessions, 
Wardha on 22.10.2002. It was registered as 
Sessions Trial No.189/2002. The charges were 
framed, and the accused persons  pleaded not 
guilty and claimed to be tried. 

--- Page 105 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 5 of 12 
 
8. The Sessions Court examined the witnesses and 
appreciated the evidence on record. It was 
observed that the injured eyewitness Vinod 
Chaudhari (PW-5) had identified the appellant 
as the driver of the jeep and he had clearly 
stated that the jeep had given a dash to the 
motorcycle from the centre part, due to which 
Ramesh Prajapati had fallen down on the road. 
Nothing had been brought on record to 
disbelieve his testimony. This testimony was 
corroborated by the seizure panchnama, the 
spot panchnama, and the testimony of the 
panch witness Gajanan (PW -3), from which it 
could be seen that the road had skid marks and 
blood stains. It was also on record that the 
motorcycle was damaged from the back, and the 
jeep, which was seized from the house of the 
accused Sanjay, was damaged on the front. It 
had also been observed that portions of broken 
indicators of the Suzuki motorcycle were found 
entangled in the front portion of the jeep.  The 
court also took into account the testimonies of 
Manoj Chaudhari (PW -6) and Deepak 

--- Page 106 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 6 of 12 
Chaudhari (PW-9) who deposed regarding prior 
enmity between the parties. Furthermore, it was 
also noted that the Medical  officers who had 
examined the complainant and the body of the 
deceased had stated that the injuries could have 
been caused by falling from the motorcycle onto 
the road. 
 
9. Based on the aforesaid, the court concluded 
that it was the appellant who was driving the 
jeep, that he had dashed into the motorcycle, 
and that he had knowledge of the fact that such 
a dash could result in the death of the 
complainant and Ramesh Prajapati . With 
regard to the co -accused persons , the court 
opined that although it was stated that they 
were passengers in the jeep, there was not 
enough evidence to show that all three accused 
persons had acted with a common intention. 
 
10. Accordingly, the court convicted the appellant, 
while acquitting the two co-accused, Sanjay and 
Vijay Ramteke. He was sentenced to undergo 
rigorous imprisonment for a period of 5 years 

--- Page 107 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 7 of 12 
under section 304-II of the IPC, and for 1 year 
under section 324 of the IPC, with both 
sentences to run concurrently. 
 
11. This order of conviction was challenged by the 
appellant before the High Court by way of filing 
Criminal Appeal No.563/2004, while the State 
filed Criminal Appeal No.735/2004 against the 
acquittal of the accused persons under sections 
302 and 307 of the IPC. 
 
12. Vide the common impugned order, the High 
Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State, 
and upheld the order of conviction of the 
appellant under sections 304-II and 324 of the 
IPC. Aggrieved, the appellant is now before us 
by way of the present appeal. 
 
13. Learned counsel for the appellant contended 
that there is no cogent or reliable evidence to 
connect the appellant with the alleged offence, 
and therefore the order of the High Court is not 
sustainable. The prosecution has not 
established beyond reasonable doubt that the 
appellant was present at the place of the 

--- Page 108 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 8 of 12 
incident and that he had knowledge that his act 
would cause the death of the deceased. 
 
14. It was submitted that in view of the previous 
enmity, the courts ought not to have believed 
the testimony of the injured eyewitness Vinod 
Chaudhari. 
 
15. It was also submitted that the courts did not 
consider that even though the incident occurred 
on a busy road, there was no independent 
eyewitness. Additionally, the truck and the auto 
driver who had taken the deceased to the 
hospital had also not been examined. 
 
16. Furthermore, it was submitted that since the 
viscera of the deceased were not preserved, the 
possibility of the deceased being in a drunken 
state and losing balance could not have been 
ruled out. 
 
17. Per contra, the learned counsel for the 
Respondent State supported the concurrent 
findings of the courts and contended that the 

--- Page 109 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 9 of 12 
offence was established beyond reasonable 
doubt qua the appellant. 
 
18. Having heard the learned counsels for the 
parties, upon consideration of the unimpeached 
testimony of the injured eyewitness Vinod 
Chaudhari(PW-5), the spot panchnama as 
proved by the testimony of Gajanan (PW-3), and 
the medical evidence, this Court was of the view 
that the appeal warranted dismissal on merits, 
and by order dated 10.04.2026 notice was 
issued limited to the question of quantum of 
sentence. 
 
19. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that 
the appellant, who was 28 years old at the time 
of the incident, is now an aged 52-year-old man. 
It is also submitted that the appellant is a 
labourer, and is the sole breadwinner of his 
family. His wife does not keep well due to certain 
ailments, and he is required to look after her 
and his children. 
 
20. This Court takes note that section 304-II of the 
IPC provides punishment in the form of 

--- Page 110 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 10 of 12 
imprisonment for a maximum term of 10 years, 
or fine, or both. 
 
21. It is also observed that the incident is that of the 
year 2002 which was 24 years ago. The 
appellant has been on bail for the majority of the 
period, having served approximately 2 months 
in custody out of the 5 years awarded. There is 
nothing that has been  brought on record to 
show that the appellant has been involved in 
any other offence in the period he has been on 
bail. 
 
22. Considering the fact that the incident being very 
old, the appellant having faced the trial, agony 
of trial, his conduct as recorded above apart 
from the fact  that the present age of the 
appellant, his ailing wife , financial condition, 
and the above stated typical facts and 
circumstances, this Court is of the view that the 
ends of justice would be served by taking a 
lenient view, and altering the quantum of 
sentence of the appellant to the period of 
custody undergone with fine of Rs.4,00,000 /-. 

--- Page 111 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 11 of 12 
We are also of the view that Rs.3,75,000/- out 
of the said amount should be paid to the legal 
representatives of the deceased as 
compensation. 
 
23. In view of the present judgment and having 
regard to the period of custody already 
undergone by the appellant, he shall not be 
required to surrender, provided he deposits the 
fine of Rs.4,00,000/ - within a period of 3 
months. The bail bonds of the appellant would 
stand cancelled on such deposit of fine. It goes 
without saying that in case of non -deposit of 
fine within the time stipulated, the present 
appeal shall fail and stand dismissed . The 
appellant shall, as a consequence, have to 
surrender and undergo the original sentence as 
imposed by the trial court on 02.09.2004. 
 
24. The present appeal is partly allowed in the 
above terms. The conviction of the appellant 
under sections 304 -II and 324 of the IPC is 
upheld and he is sentenced to the period 
undergone, with a fine of Rs.4,00,000 /-, 

--- Page 112 ---
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.6358/2026                                          Page 12 of 12 
Rs.3,75,000/- out of which is to be paid to the 
legal representatives of the deceased. 
 
25. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.  ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. PS Patwalia, learned senior counsel for the
appellants; Mohd Irshad, learned Additional Advocate General for
the State of Punjab; and Mr. R.K. Jain, learned senior counsel for
the informants- respondent Nos.2 and 3.
3. The related Special Leave Petition has been filed against the
condition imposed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana (High
Court) while granting anticipatory bail to the appellants. The
offending condition reads thus:
27. So, the concession of bail is further
subject  to  deposit  of  an  amount  of
Rs.4,00,00,000/- (Rupees Four Crores), in the
Court of the Area Magistrate or with the
Investigating Officer in the form of a Fixed
Deposit Receipt (FDR) from a nationalized
bank,  wherever  dispute  remains  pending,
within a period of six months from today.
Petitioners are directed to ensure that the
1

--- Page 126 ---
said FDR is renewed at least one week prior
to its expiry, until such time as it is
encashed by the concerned party.
It is further clarified that the FDR with
its matured amount shall be encashed by the
concerned party subject to the final decision
in  the  case  by  the  competent  court,  or
alternatively, if the dispute is resolved
amicably between the parties.
4. Appellants are accused in FIR No.78 of 2022 registered at
Police Station Phase-1 S.A.S. Nagar, (Mohali) under Sections 406,
420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
Shorn of details, as per the allegation made in the FIR, appellants
have duped the informants of a substantial sum of money which the
informants had invested through them for purchase of an industrial
estate at Mohali in the State of Punjab. It is not necessary at
this stage to go into the minute details of the allegations against
the appellants in as much as grant of anticipatory bail by the High
Court to the appellants have not been assailed either by the State
or by the informants. 
5. In the impugned order, the High Court noted that informants
have already instituted a suit for specific performance being Civil
Suit No.265 of 2024 pending in the Court of Civil Judge, Senior
Division, S.A.S. Nagar- Mohali; the allegations and materials
disclose a dispute having a predominantly civil flavour. By the
impugned order dated 22.12.2025 the appellants have been granted
the benefit of pre-arrest bail but on the condition, extracted
2

--- Page 127 ---
supra.
6. While disposing of the matter, the High Court observed that
the investigation should be expedited whereafter the Trial Court
should finally be decided within one year.
7. This Court by order dated 13.04.2026, issued notice and stayed
the condition of depositing 4,00,00,000/- (Rupees four crores₹
only) as a condition precedent for bail. However, this Court
directed the appellants to file an undertaking before the Trial
Court that they would not transfer the properties any further.
8. Mr. Patwalia, learned senior counsel submits that in so far
the undertaking directed by this Court is concerned, the same has
already been filed. He submits that the High Court has also
accepted the contention of the appellant that the dispute between
the informant and the appellants is primarily civil in nature and
therefore had granted anticipatory bail to the appellant. However,
the High Court could not have imposed the condition of deposit of
4,00,00,000/-  (Rupees  four  crores  only).  In  support  of  his₹
contention, he has placed reliance on the following judgments: 
I.  Munish Bhasin v. State NCT of Delhi (2009)
4 SCC 45.
II. Ramesh Kumar v. State NCT of Delhi (2023)
7 SCC 461.
III. Pratnik Kumar v. State of Jharkhand SLP
(Crl) D.No.4297/2026.
IV. Gajanan  Dattatray  Gore  v.  State  of
Maharashtra & Anr.
8.1. On the strength of the above decided cases, Mr. Patwalia,
3

--- Page 128 ---
learned senior counsel submits that this Court may set aside the
condition of deposit of 4,00,00,000/- (Rupees four crores only) as₹
imposed by the High Court while granting anticipatory bail to the
appellants.
9. Learned Additional Advocate General for the State of Punjab
referring to the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the State
submits that investigation is complete whereafter the final report
in the form of charge sheet has been prepared which would be
presented before the Court shortly.
10. Mr.  Jain,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the  informants-
respondent Nos. 2 and 3 submits that respondent No.2 is now more
than 90 years old. It is an admitted fact that she has been duped
by the appellants. Though the transaction in question took place
about 15-16 years ago, she is still awaiting justice in this case.
Therefore,  the  High  Court  after  noticing  the  plight  of  the
informants, imposed the aforesaid condition of deposit of money to
balance the interest on both the parties. In so far the judgments
of this Court is concerned, learned senior counsel submits that
each case turns on its own facts. In a matter relating to grant of
bail, regular or anticipatory, the Court has the discretion to
impose such conditions as it thinks necessary for furthering the
cause of justice. Therefore, no interference is called for.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties have
received the due consideration of the Court. 
12. As already noted above, facts are not in dispute. The only
issue is regarding legality and validity of the condition imposed
4

--- Page 129 ---
by the High Court directing the appellants to deposit an amount of
4,00,00,000/- (Rupees four crores only) before the concerned₹
magistrate as a condition precedent for grant of anticipatory bail.
13. In Munish Bhasin, this Court observed that while exercising
discretion to release an accused under Section 438 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, ‘CrPC’) neither the High Court
nor the Sessions Court would be justified in imposing freakish
conditions.  Though  the  Court  has  the  discretion  to  impose
necessary, just and efficacious conditions while enlarging an
accused on bail under Section 438 CrPC but the accused cannot be
subjected to any irrelevant condition at all. Paragraph 12 of the
said judgment reads as follows:
12. While imposing conditions on an accused
who approaches the court under Section 438 of
the Code, the Court should be extremely chary
in imposing the conditions which are not
called for at all. There is no manner of
doubt that the conditions to be imposed under
Section 438 of the Code cannot be harsh,
onerous or excessive so as to frustrate the
very object of grant of anticipatory bail
under Section 438 of the code.
14. This Court in  Ramesh Kumar  considered this issue in an
exhaustive manner. This Court noted that a disquieting trend
emerging over the years which has gained pace in recent times has
necessitated the rendering of the opinion. It has been found that
in multiple cases where FIRs were lodged under Section 420 IPC,
judicial proceedings initiated by the accused under Section 438
5

--- Page 130 ---
CrPC are unwittingly being transformed into processes for recovery
of the quantum of money allegedly cheated and the courts driven to
impose conditions for deposit/payment as prerequisite for grant of
pre-arrest bail.
14.1. After referring to various decisions, this Court observed
that in the context of grant of bail, all such conditions that
would  facilitate  the  appearance  of  the  accused  before  the
investigating officer or the trial court, would be  relevant and
should only be imposed. However, inclusion of a condition for
payment of money by the accused for bail tends to create an
impression that bail can be secured by depositing money alleged to
have been cheated. This is really not the purpose and intent of the
provision for grant of bail. 
14.2. Clarifying the position, this Court observed that in
exceptional cases, such as, where an allegation of misappropriation
of public money by the accused is levelled and the accused while
seeking indulgence of the court to have his liberty secured,
volunteers to make good the money allegedly misappropriated by him,
it would be open to the Court concerned to consider whether in the
larger public interest the money allegedly misappropriated should
be allowed to be deposited before the application for anticipatory
bail or regular bail, as the case may be, is taken up for
consideration. However, such an effort would not be warranted in
cases of private disputes where private parties complain of their
money being involved in the offence of cheating. 
15. This Court in Gajanan Dattatray Gore held as follows:
6

--- Page 131 ---
24. Be that at it may, now we have made
ourselves very clear that there shall not be
a single order that the High Courts and the
Trial Courts shall pass for grant of regular
bail or anticipatory bail on the basis of any
accused or his/her family members giving an
undertaking to deposit a particular amount.
The plea shall be decided strictly on merits
in accordance with law. If the case is made
out on merits the court may exercise its
discretion and if no case is made out on
merits, the court shall reject the plea for
regular bail or anticipatory bail as the case
may be. However, in any circumstances the
High Courts or trial courts shall not pass a
conditional  order  of  regular  bail  or
anticipatory bail.
 
16.  Though the High Court had relied upon a judgment of this
Court in  Subhelal Alias Sushil Sahu vs. State of Chhattisgarh
(2025) 5 SCC 140, that was a case of crypto currency scam in which
almost 2,000 investors had lost their money in the scheme floated
by the accused persons. In the peculiar facts of that case whether
the interest of a large number of depositors were involved, this
Court directed the accused to deposit an amount of 35,00,000/-₹
(rupees thirty five lakhs only) before the Trial Court. However,
while directing so, this Court observed as under: 
26. We are conscious of the fact that we have
been condemning the High Courts when they
impose such conditions. But here is a case
wherein  we  are  compelled  to  impose  such
7

--- Page 132 ---
conditions  having  regard  to  the  peculiar
facts of this case.
17. We are, therefore, of the considered opinion that the decision
in Subhelal Alias Sushil Sahu, would not be attracted to the facts
of this case.
18. When the High Court came to the conclusion that a case for
anticipatory bail is made out, it ought not to have imposed such a
condition as a pre-condition for bail. 
19. Having regard to the above and on due consideration, we set
aside the condition imposed by the High Court for depositing
4,00,00,000/- (Rupees four crores only)₹  by the appellants as
extracted supra, as a condition precedent for grant of pre-arrest
bail.
20. We feel that the undertaking given by the appellants before
this Court in terms of our order dated 13.04.2026 that appellants
would  not  transfer  the  properties  any  further,  is  actually
redundant in as much as the Civil Court in the pending civil suit
has already directed by order dated 20.12.2024 that the defendants
(appellants herein) shall not alienate the suit property any
further. Therefore, the undertaking given by the appellants in
terms of the order of this Court would stand merged with the order
of the Civil Court.
21. Since investigation is complete, we direct the prosecution to
submit charge sheet within 2 weeks from today whereafter the
parties may avail their respective remedies in accordance with law.
22. The appeal is accordingly allowed.
8

23. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. These  appeals would  call in  question the  order
passed by the High Court dismissing the writ petition(s)
filed by the present appellant(s), which in turn had called
in question the order passed by the Appellate Authority
under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (for short ‘the
Act’) dated 24.03.2023, by setting aside the order passed
by the Controlling Authority under the Act dated 18.04.2022
allowing the gratuity claims of the appellant(s) in the
1

--- Page 145 ---
following manner:
Name of the Petitioner Amount of gratuity
Prabhat Kumar Singh 3,79,817/-
Anil Sahadeo Kadam 2,99,538/-
Nilesh Afre 3,74,867/-
Shrikant B. Chinchkar 2,06,630/-
3. Admittedly, the appellant(s) were employed in the
respondent company, in its Production Planning and Control
Department,  since  the  year  2007  onwards.  All  the
appellant(s) resigned from their posts by tendering letters
of  resignation  on  different  dates.  The  resignation
submitted by Prabhat Kumar Singh only was accepted on
03.10.2018 to be made effective from 03.11.2018, when he
was to be relieved. In respect of other appellant(s), their
resignations were never accepted.
4. While it being so, the appellant(s) were issued a
letter of termination on 14.11.2018, which was not preceded
by  any  inquiry.  Prior  to  this,  on  05.11.2018,  the
appellant(s) were issued a show-cause notice as to why, on
account of their act of misconduct in causing damage and
loss to the company, the amount of gratuity payable to them
may not be forfeited to the extent of the aforesaid amount
of loss, which was mentioned as Rs.50 Lakhs in the said
notice.
5. It is the case of the respondent company that the
appellant(s) never submitted any reply to this notice,
which enabled them to withhold the gratuity payable to the
2

--- Page 146 ---
appellant(s), while settling their claims.
6. The appellant(s) thereafter moved an application
under Section 8 of the Act for payment of gratuity, which
was allowed by the Controlling Authority on 18.04.2022,
holding that the requirement under Section 4(6)(b)(ii) for
forfeiting the amount of gratuity was not fully complied
with. It was found that the FIR filed by the company
against the appellant(s) does not give any authority to the
employer to withhold their amount of gratuity because, as
per  Section  4(6)(b)(ii),  the  misconduct  has  to  be
established as an offense involving moral turpitude for
which the employee has to be convicted by a court of
competent jurisdiction.
7. It was also observed that in the absence of any
specific allegations or charge for causing pecuniary loss
to the respondent company, gratuity cannot be forfeited.
The above order of the Controlling Authority was challenged
before the Appellate Authority, which was allowed by order
dated 24.03.2023, and the High Court has affirmed this
order.
8. It is argued that there is absolutely not an iota of
evidence as to the extent of loss the respondent company
has suffered. Therefore, the prerequisite of withholding of
gratuity to the extent of loss suffered by the company has
not been satisfied under Section 4(6)(b)(ii) of the Act. It
is submitted that admittedly no inquiry was conducted
before terminating the appellant(s)’ services. Therefore,
3

--- Page 147 ---
there was no occasion either for the company to prove the
extent of loss, nor was there any opportunity for the
appellant(s) to disprove the claim of the company in the
absence of an inquiry.
9. Per contra, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
respondent company, would take us through the statement of
the appellant(s) recorded during the proceedings before the
Controlling Authority. According to him the appellant(s)
having accepted the misconduct in their cross-examination,
the company was entitled to forfeit the gratuity. It is
also submitted that as per their own admission, they used
to procure goods at Rs.3,600 from a supplier company and
sell it to the respondent company at Rs.6,900. Therefore,
the difference between these two prices is the extent of
loss suffered by the respondent company, and no further
proof was required.
10. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and on
examination of the material on record, we find that the
appellant(s)' termination, having not been preceded with
any  inquiry,  the  appellant(s)  were  not  given  any
opportunity to contest the company's claim about the loss
suffered by it.
11. Moreover, the FIR lodged by the respondent company
against the appellant(s) was investigated and closed by the
jurisdictional Investigating Officer, in its report dated
05.02.2020, with a finding which is reproduced hereunder:
“During the investigation of the
4

--- Page 148 ---
said crime, it was found that Accused
Nos. 1 to 4, with the implied or verbal
permission  of  the  complainant,
established a company named “Make Craft
Industrial Company" in the name of the
complainant's wife. The said company
obtained  work  orders  from  the
complainant's company and, according to
the orders, got the goods manufactured
from another company and fulfilled the
complainant's  company’s  orders.  In
return,  they  received  an  amount  of
Rs.11,90,244  from  the  complainant’s
company, while an outstanding amount of
Rs.3,01,400 is yet to be received by
the  accused.  Therefore,  the
investigation revealed that there was
no financial loss or misappropriation
to the complainant.  However, it was
found that the accused established a
separate company in the name of the
complainant's wife without his direct
involvement. This matter is of a civil
nature, and since the crime is of a
civil nature, Asst. Sub-Inspector V.A.
Dabholkar  has  submitted  a  request
report for summary approval.
Sub-Divisional Police Officer,
Vashi  Division,  has  submitted  a
recommendation for summary approval of
the  documents  related  to  the  case
registered as Crime No. I-290/2018 at
Rabale  MIDC  Police  Station  under
Sections 420, 406, and 34 of the IPC,
considering it as a civil matter.
After a thorough examination
of  the  investigation  documents,
permission is granted to present the
'Civil Summary' of Crime No. 290/2018
registered  at  Rabale  MIDC  Police
Station under Sections 420, 406, and 34
of the IPC before the Hon'ble Court.
The  original  reference
5

--- Page 149 ---
documents are attached herewith.”
12. It is also significant to notice that in its show-
cause notice dated 05.11.2018 issued to the appellant(s),
the respondent company quantified the net loss suffered by
the company to the extent of not less than Rs.50 Lakhs.
However, there was no accompanying document in the form of
calculation or audit report which would substantiate the
claim of the company about the loss suffered. In any case,
such computation or assessment of loss has to be presented
before the Controlling Authority, which too was not done by
the respondent company.
13. It is for the company to have proved the financial
loss  suffered  by  it  due  to  the  misconduct  of  the
appellant(s), and they cannot take benefit of statements
made by the appellant(s) in their cross-examination in the
proceedings before the Controlling Authority. The financial
loss suffered by the company has to be proved by producing
independent evidence before the Controlling Authority. Even
before this Court, no such document has been submitted with
the counter-affidavit of the respondent.
14. In the matter of Permali Wallance Ltd. v. State of
Madhya Pradesh1, the High Court of Madhya Pradesh has taken
a view that the right of the employer to forfeit the amount
of earned gratuity of an employee whose services were
terminated for any act, willful omission, or negligence
causing any damage to the employer is limited to the extent
1. (1996) 2 LLJ 515,
6

--- Page 150 ---
of damage and the proof of such damage. We are in agreement
with the view taken by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, as
we have independently found that the respondent company has
failed to submit any proof of extent of damage suffered by
it by submitting documents in support of such claim by the
company.
15. To the contrary, in the FIR filed by the company, a
closure report has been submitted finding that there was no
financial loss or misappropriation committed against the
respondent company.
16. In view of the above, we are inclined to allow the
appeal(s), set aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court and the Appellate Authority, and restore the order
passed by the Controlling Authority on 18.04.2022.
17. The order passed by the Controlling Authority shall
be complied with within a period of two months from today.
18. The appeal(s) stand allowed in the above terms.
19. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 171626/2026:
1. This is an application seeking recall of the order dated
08.05.2026 directing that the post of Secretary, SCBA in the 2026-
27 elections be set apart exclusively for women candidates.  
2. The contention of the applicants is that in the earlier order
dated 02.05.2024, it was directed that the posts of Office bearers
by rotation was to be kept apart for women.  It is further
contended  that,  by  order  dated  27.04.2026,  for  the  2026-27
election, the post of Vice-President was directed to be kept apart
exclusively for women candidates.  The applicants contend that on
08.05.2026, the order of 27.04.2026 was modified and the post of
Secretary was kept apart exclusively for women candidates for the
7

--- Page 160 ---
2026-27 elections.  
3. We find absolutely no merit in the contentions, and we find no
ground to recall the order of 08.05.2026.
4. First of all, as the order dated 08.05.2026 makes it clear
that there was overwhelming desire from the members of the Bar
especially the women members of the Bar that for the election of
2026-27, the post of Secretary should be earmarked.  It was
mentioned further that the SCBA General Body may consider the
desirability of creating one additional post of Vice-President and
Joint Secretary to be exclusively reserved for women.  It was in
the  said  circumstances  that  the  order  dated  27.04.2026  was
modified.  Further, on 27.04.2026, the election schedule has been
already notified, and the polling is due on 18.08.2026.
5. For the afore-stated reasons, we find no merit in the IA and
the same stands dismissed.
(ARJUN BISHT)                               (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Dr. S. Muralidhar, the learned Amicus has placed on record a
detailed Status Report.
2. In the Status Report, the learned Amicus has provided the
background of the entire litigation, more particularly the various
directions issued by this Court in its decision titled “Sukanya
Shantha vs. Union of India and Others”, reported in (2024) 15 SCC
535.

--- Page 188 ---
5
3. The report talks about compliance of various directions issued
by this Court in the Judgment, referred to above, including the
clarificatory Order passed by this Court dated 7th November, 2024.
4. We have looked into the entire report. One copy of the Status
Report has been provided to all other learned Counsel appearing in
this litigation.
5. However, in the course of today's hearing, learned Amicus laid
much stress on para 25 of his status report. 
Para 25 is titled 'Information Awaited 
Para 25 reads thus:-
The AC is awaiting further written responses from several
States/UTs in respect of:-
a. The method of collection and transmission of caste-data to
NCRB;
b. Deletion of caste columns in all the registers and forms in
prisons;
c.  Outsourcing of cleaning work;
d. Status of compliance with the guidelines in the judgments in
Arnesh Kumar and Amanatullah Khan;
    e. Notifications constituting BoVs district wise;
   f. Status of new Acts/Rules/Manuals that are proposed by several 
States/UTs;
  g.  Status  of  amendments  to  offending  provisions  in  the  
Acts/Rules/Manuals.”
6. As regards the information which the learned Amicus seeks, we
requested Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, the learned Additional Solicitor
General, to look into the same and take up the matter with all
States and Union Territories and try to gather the necessary
information at the earliest.
7. The learned Amicus made us understand that the State of Assam,
the State of Madhya Pradesh, the State of Meghalaya, and the Union
Territory of Chandigarh have evolved a methodology insofar as
collection and transmission of caste data is concerned. According

--- Page 189 ---
6
to him, the same methodology may be adopted by other States/UTs for
the purpose of procuring the necessary information.  
8. The learned Amicus also brought something very important to
our notice. According to him, as on date, none of the States/Union
Territories  has  constituted  Board  of  Visitors  District-wise.
According to him, it is very much important and necessary for each
State/UT to constitute Board of Visitors in each of the Districts
where are sub-jails.
9. This has to be done under the Model Prison Manual, 2016, more
particularly, Clause 29.01 read with 29.03 respectively including
the State Prison Manual respectively.
10. We direct all the State Governments/Union Territories to
ensure that Board of Visitors is constituted district – wise headed
by the Principal District Judge of that particular District, within
a period of four weeks from today. Board of Visitors shall be
constituted accordingly without fail. Any laxity in this regard
will be viewed strictly. 
11. We request Ms. Bhati to see that the each of the States/Union
Territories are conveyed as regards the direction issued today by
this Court for the purpose of constituting the Board of Visitors
District-wise.
12. We also direct all the States/Union Territories to provide us
the status of amendments to the offending provisions in the
Acts/Rules/Manuals as pointed out by the learned Amicus in his
Status Report within a period of four weeks from today.
13. Registry shall forward one copy each of this Order to the
Principal Secretary (Home) of all the States/Lieutenant Governors
of Union Territories. The necessary Report as regards the aforesaid
shall be forwarded by the respective States/Union Territories by
3-9-2026. Once all the necessary information is received, the
Registry shall provide one copy each to the learned Amicus at the
earliest.
13. By Order dated 15-12-2025, we had taken note of relief prayed
for  in  one  interim  application  preferred  by  the  applicant
concerned. 

--- Page 190 ---
7
14. In the said interim application, relief prayed for seeking
direction  to  all  the  States  to  file  appropriate  affidavits
concerning any similar provisions and to produce Police Regulations
and/or Standing Orders and/or Rules and/or any other subordinate
legislation  concerning  policing  before  this  Court  and  issue
appropriate directions in that regard.
15. Insofar as this prayer is concerned, we had observed that we
will have to hear all the States and Union Territories which may
take a long time. In such circumstances, we request the Union of
India to look into it and file its reply in this regard before the
next date of hearing.
16. Post this matter on 10-9-2026.

  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(C) No. 9275/2026)
SHAILENDRA AGRAWAL & ANR.                            Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
ADDITIONAL COLLECTOR AND ADDITIONAL MAGISTRATE & ORS.Respondent(s)
     O R D E R
1. Delay in re-filing is condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. This appeal would call in question the order
passed by the Division Bench of the High Court,
affirming the order passed by the Single Judge
wherein, the appellant(s) had prayed for setting
aside  of  the  order  passed  by  the  Additional
Collector, Kanadia on 22.02.2022 and the FIR being
Crime No.153/2022 at Police Station-Kanadia for
offences punishable under Sections 406, 420, 467,
468, 120-B and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(for short, 'the Act'). 
4. The  High  Court  has  observed  that  the
complaint  was  filed  by  the  fourth  respondent
alleging that appellant(s) are selling plots and
receiving money without completing the development
of  the  colony.  While  considering  the  said
complaint, the Additional Collector passed the

--- Page 192 ---
2
order  holding  that  as  per  the  Memorandum  of
Understanding dated 10.09.2007, the right to sell
the plots is only available with the landowner
i.e. the fourth respondent therein, and also that
the  completion  certificate  has  wrongly  been
obtained from the SDO and the mortgaged plots were
fraudulently redeemed. Basing these observations,
the  Additional  Collector  also  directed  for
registration of an FIR against the appellant(s).
5. The High Court observed that since an FIR
has already been registered, no interference can
be made even if the order dated 22.02.2022 of the
Additional  Collector  is  treated  as  without
authority or declared illegal.
6. In the counter affidavit dated 27.07.2026
filed by the respondent Nos.1 and 2-State of
Madhya Pradesh, it is stated thus in paragraph
nos-20 to 23:
“20. It  is  submitted  that  upon
examination of the material on record,
Respondent No. 1 passed the order dated
22.02.2022 in Revenue Case No. 145/B-
121/21-22,  recording  a  prima  facie
finding of fraud and misrepresentation in
the procurement of the release of the
mortgaged plots, and directing Respondent
No. 2 to inform the police authorities so
that the criminal law could be set in
motion.
21. It is submitted that pursuant to the
said  order,  FIR  No.  153/2022  was
registered at Police Station Kanadiya on
24.02.2022 for offences under Sections
406, 420, 467,468, 120-B and 34 of the
Indian Penal Code.

--- Page 193 ---
3
22.  It is submitted that the Petitioners
challenged the order dated 22.02.2022 by
way of Writ Petition No. 7754 of 2022
before the Hon'ble High Court of Madhya
Pradesh, which came to be dismissed by
the learned Single Judge vide order dated
27.01.2025,  upholding  the  action  of
Respondent No. 1.
23. It is submitted that it may be noted
that  Respondent  No.1  subsequently
disposed of Revenue Case No.145/B-121/21-
22 vide order dated 07.11.2024, for want
of subject-matter jurisdiction over the
question of allotment of plots to colony
members  inter  se,  which  is  a  matter
triable by a civil court and distinct
from the commission of the cognizable
offences  disclosed  by  the  record  and
independently taken cognizance of by the
investigating agency.”
7. From the above statement made in the counter
affidavit,  it  is  abundantly  clear  that  the
gravamen of the application filed by the private
respondent(s) before the Additional Collector was
concerning release of the mortgaged plots and
failure  of  the  appellant(s)  to  carry  out
development work, which was rightly found by the
State to be a matter triable by the Civil Court,
as  stated  in  Paragraph  No.23  of  the  counter
affidavit filed by the State of Madhya Pradesh.
Once the State is of the view that the dispute
between the parties, brought before the Additional
Collector, is a matter triable by the Civil Court,
the consequent action of the Additional Collector

--- Page 194 ---
4
in lodging the FIR against the appellant(s) has to
fail.
8. At this stage, learned Additional Advocate
General,  Mr. Sridhar Potaraju, appearing for the
State, would point out that in the Writ Petition
preferred before the Single Judge, the only prayer
was for quashing of the order passed by the
Additional Collector and not the FIR/Crime Number
and it is in this factual position, the High Court
has  found  that  once  an  FIR/Crime  Number  is
registered, quashing of the order passed by the
Additional Collector would not set aside the FIR/
Crime Number registered for a cognizable offence.
9. In  our  considered  view,  once  an  order
passed by the Additional Collector is the basis
for registering an FIR/Crime Number and on State’s
own  admission,  if  that  order  was  without
jurisdiction as it involved a civil dispute, the
FIR registered on the basis of the said order has
to go and the same cannot be continued in the
teeth of the admission made by the State.
10. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  is  set
aside.  The  appeal  stands  allowed  and  it  is
directed that the FIR being Crime No.153/2022
registered at Police Station-Kanadia is quashed as
the same arises out of a civil dispute.

5
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The State of Himachal Pradesh has filed a Compliance
Report, suggesting that the selection process for appointment of
Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioner(s) in
the State has been completed. However, the result of the selection
process could not be notified owing to the recently-concluded
Municipal Elections.  
2. In our considered view, the Model Code of Conduct being
in force during the elections could not be construed as an
impediment to matters concerning statutory appointments, especially
when the same was required to be done under this Court’s directions
in a time-bound manner.  
3. Consequently, irrespective of the Model Code of Conduct

--- Page 202 ---
5
being in force, we direct the State Government to notify the result
of the selection process and make appointments within two weeks. A
Compliance Affidavit be filed in this regard.
4. So far as the State of Jharkhand is concerned, a Status
Report has been handed over during the course of hearing. As per
the  Report,  only  four  Information  Commissioners  have  been
appointed. Three more appointments, including that of the Chief
Information Officer, are required to be made. Para 9 of the
affidavit  indicates  that  the  applications  have  already  been
received for the post of Chief Information Commissioner.
5. Accordingly, let the said process be finalised within two
months, and a Compliance Affidavit be filed after making the
appointments.
6. Regarding the State of Maharashtra, learned standing
counsel informs us that the file regarding the creation of three
more posts of State Information Commissioners has been cleared by
the Finance Department and that the selection process will be
completed within two months.
7. Let the three vacancies be notified within one week,
whereupon an endeavour shall be made to complete the selection
process within two months from the date of issuance of the
advertisement.
8. In our considered opinion, the functioning of the State
Information  Commission  in  the  State  of  Bihar  is  far  from
satisfactory. There are 36,000 pending appeals and only three
Information Commissioners are functioning. One existing post is
lying vacant, and very few steps have been taken to fill up the
same.  
9. We have been informed that an advertisement for filling
up the vacant post has been issued. Let the said post be filled up
by completing the selection process within one month. Similarly,
keeping in view the total pendency, the State Government is
directed to create three more posts of Information Commissioners
and the process  re: creation  be completed within two months
thereafter.  The  newly-created  posts  shall  also  be  advertised

--- Page 203 ---
6
without any delay.
10. As regards the State of Chhattisgarh, we are informed
that four Information Commissioners are now functioning. During the
last  hearing,  we  were  informed  that  the  total  pendency  of
complaints  as  well  as  appeals  before  the  State  Information
Commission was 52,000, which is stated to have been slightly
reduced as of now.  
11. We, accordingly, direct the State of Chhattisgarh to
revisit the strength of the State Information Commission and
consider the appointment of additional Information Commissioners to
aid in the disposal of pending complaints/appeals. A decision, in
this regard, be taken within one month.
12. Despite the directions issued in para 11 of the order
dated 10.02.2026, the State of Assam has not appointed a Chief
Information Commissioner. Learned counsel for the State again
assures us that the appointment shall be made within one month.  We
direct that the post of Chief Information Commissioner be filled
within one month, and a Compliance Affidavit be filed.  
13. In  the  State  of  Tamil  Nadu,  while  four  Information
Commissioners are already functioning, the posts for the remaining
four Information Commissioners as well as the Chief Information
Commissioner are lying vacant. Learned counsel, on instructions,
states that the selection process for the post of Chief Information
Commissioner and the pending four Information Commissioners has
already commenced and the same shall be completed within two
months. Let a Compliance Affidavit be filed in this regard. 
14. During the course of hearing, we are informed that in the
State of Rajasthan, there is no Chief Information Commissioner. The
State Government is, accordingly, directed to take necessary steps
for appointment of the State Chief Information Commissioner within
two months.
15. Finally, we direct that the details of all the newly-
appointed Chief Information Commissioners/Information Commissioners
be uploaded on the respective websites of the State Information
Commissions.

2

being the only other co-accused whereas the

on record.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        of 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No.25495 of 2025) 
RANCHI MUNICIPAL CORPORATION         …. APPELLANT (S)

A 2 Z WASTE MANAGEMENT (RANCHI) 
LIMITED                  …. RESPONDENT(S)
With
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        of 2026
(Arising out of SLP(C) No. 26045 of 2025)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2.  The appellant-Ranchi  Municipal  Corporation,  is the respondent
and  the  respondent  herein,  a  Special  Purpose  Vehicle  (SPV)
constituted to carry out the subject contract, is the claimant before
the Arbitration Tribunal. The Tribunal found both the parties to be
guilty of breach of different aspects of the contract; the appellant for
not having handed over possession of the land for construction of
structures and levy of penalty, which was deducted from the bills,
while  the  respondent  had  failed  to  perform  some  parts  of  the
contractual  obligations  which  were  vital  for  the  maintenance  of
hygiene, affecting the health of citizens of the town of Ranchi. 
3.    The  claim  for  Capital  Grant  raised  under  two  heads  were
rejected  by  the  Tribunal.  The  claimant  was  found  entitled  to

--- Page 227 ---
Rs.1,71,95,156/- (Rupees One crore seventy one lakh ninety five
thousand one hundred and fifty six only) as tipping charges and
while the claim for damages for loss of profit was declined, nominal
damages were awarded amounting to Rs.2,00,00,000/- (Rupees Two
crores only). The claimant was also found entitled to 15% interest
per annum on the tipping charges and the damages. The total cost
for arbitration was fixed at Rs.55,00,000/- (Rupees Fifty five lakh)
which  is not under  challenge.  The counterclaim was confined  to
Rs.17,65,166/-  (Rupees  Seventeen  lakh  sixty  five  thousand  one
hundred and sixty six only), found entitled to the appellant. The
breach found on the part of the claimant was compensated by the
encashment of bank guarantee furnished by the claimant, which was
deemed to be the damages for breach as entitled to the respondent.
4. The Arbitral Award was challenged by the appellant under Section
34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 1 in which the entire
award was set aside as per Annexure P-3. The Commercial Court,
Ranchi,  in  Annexure  P-3  found  that  under  Capital  Grants,  the
claimant raised invoices with respect to purchase of vehicles, many
of which were found to be bogus. The Tribunal also found fraud
having  been  employed  insofar  as  the  said  purchase  invoices
produced. Finding that fraud vitiates everything, the entire award
was set aside on the reasoning that the tipping fee related to the
1  Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’

--- Page 228 ---
collection and transportation of waste in vehicles, which were never
purchased and hence the billing itself was fraudulent. The claimant
approached the High Court under Section 37 of the Act in which the
finding of the Commercial Court that the entire claims were vitiated
by fraud was set aside and the award restored. The fraud found on
the part of acquisition of capital goods need not be mixed up with
the payments towards bills raised for the regular operation of solid
waste disposal carried out, was the reasoning. 
5.   The appellant-Corporation is before us challenging the order
under Section 37 of the Act.  As has been found in the order of the
Commercial Court itself, the jurisdiction is very circumscribed. We
agree with the High Court that the fraud found by the Tribunal is on
purchase of vehicles as a capital acquisition for the project itself
which  was  to  be  continued  for  30  years,  if  it  had  not  been
terminated.  The  contract  was  not  only  for  collection  and
transportation of waste but also to develop, construct, operate and
maintain municipal solid waste processing facilities with compost
plant and any other suitable processing plants with a sanitary landfill
facility at the city of Ranchi through Public Private Partnership under
JnNURM Scheme. Hence, the finding that the bogus purchase would
vitiate the entire claim cannot be sustained. 
6.  In this context we also have to notice that the Tribunal while
allowing the claim of tipping fee, specifically observed in Paragraph

--- Page 229 ---
428 of the Award that ‘ the calculations made by the claimant on the
aforementioned  dues,  is  not  in  dispute’.  Hence  the  award  of
Rs.1,71,95,156/-  stands sustained. The Award of 15% interest is as
per the contract and there is no reason to interfere with that too.
7.  Insofar as damages are concerned, the Tribunal found breach of
some  aspects  on  the  claimant  and  some  other  aspects  on  the
respondent.  The  respondent  was  found  entitled  to  encashment
made of the bank guarantee provided. The claim of damages for loss
of profit was declined and only a nominal damage of Two crores was
awarded.  It  was  found  in  Paragraph  400  of  the  award  that  the
contract was on a long-term basis and even the first phase of the
contract was not completed. It was found that there is no reason to
apply restitutionary principles for the purpose of computation of loss
of  profit  and  hence,  the  nominal  award  of  Two  crores.  We  find
absolutely no reason to interfere with it, but the aspect of breach
having been found on both and the award having declined damages
on loss of profit, as claimed by the claimant, we are of the opinion
that there  is  no  reason  to  mulct that  liability  with  interest.  The
interest of 15 % as awarded for the amount of damages stands
deleted.
8.  The impugned judgment is modified to the above extent.
9.   The Appeals stand disposed of leaving the parties to bear their
respective costs.
